source.title_on_document: Augmenting Research Ideation with Data: An Empirical Investigation in Social Science

supplement.where: Appendices A–K, pp. 11–25 of this PDF.
supplement.holds: Datasets, research topics, generation methods, evaluation criteria, implementation details, a hypothesis-validation pilot, examples, prompts, evaluator agreement, and study interfaces. Appendix I.2 (p. 18) gives the human-task duration; Figure 4 (p. 25) shows its interface. The appendices do not state random assignment or a separate analyzed human-ideator count, and do not provide uncertainty estimates for Table 6a.

paper_design_summary: The human study recruited 23 people from a social science course; each chose two climate-negotiation topics and proposed an idea for each, with LLM-generated references for one and Internet/literature search without LLMs for the other (pp. 7–8, §6.1). Experts compared the ideas on overall quality, novelty, feasibility, significance and expected effectiveness; allocation of topics to assistance conditions and condition order are not stated (p. 8, §6.2 and Table 6a; p. 18, Appendix I.2; p. 25, Figure 4). Other experiments assess metadata in model idea generation, validation in model idea selection, and automated hypothesis validation; the five extracted outcomes below concern the human-produced ideas (pp. 4–7, §§4–5; pp. 14–15, Appendix F).

studies.label: Human research ideation (§6; within-person comparison, assignment not stated)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Each participant chose two of four topics, received AI-generated references for one, and received no references for the other. The paper does not explain which topic received references or how condition order was determined. Random sampling in §6.2 concerns pairing surplus ideas for evaluation, not assigning assistance to people.
assignment.quote: For one of the two topics, participants are provided with three reference ideas, accompanied by data snippets used in automatic validation and the validation processes.
assignment.locator: pp. 7–8, §6.1, Experiment Design; p. 8, §6.2, Quality of Ideas; p. 18, Appendix I.2; p. 25, Figure 4.

arms.name: With references
arms.description: For one selected topic, the participant receives three LLM-generated research ideas, data snippets, and raw and summarized validation processes. This is one condition experienced by the same recruited cohort; analyzed arm counts are not separately reported (p. 8, §6.1).

arms.name: Without references
arms.description: For the other selected topic, the participant receives no reference ideas, may browse the Internet and search the literature, and may not use LLMs. This is the other condition experienced by the same cohort; analyzed arm counts are not separately reported (p. 8, §6.1).

participants.who: 23 participants were recruited from a social science course: 19 undergraduate or graduate students and 4 senior researchers holding a PhD in a related field. The paper does not separately report the number analyzed, so n_analyzed and the analyzed arm counts are null; 23 is the recruitment count, not a verified post-exclusion count.
participants.quote: We recruit 23 participants from a social science course to take part in the study.
participants.locator: p. 7, §6.1, Experiment Design; p. 3, Introduction (study with 23 researchers); p. 8, §6.2 and Table 6a (results without a separate analyzed headcount).

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-Researcher using GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-08-06), with ideas selected by Claude-3.5-Sonnet (claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022).
ai_tool.how_used: Participants view supplied research ideas generated with CLIMATEDATABANK metadata and selected using automatic validation, together with data snippets and validation traces; the treatment is supplied references rather than open chatbot use (p. 8, §6.1; p. 5, §4.3, Implementation Details and model-version footnote).

task.description: Select two personally interesting climate-negotiation topics from four offered topics, then propose a research idea for each, comprising a research question, theory and hypotheses (pp. 7–8, §6.1; p. 25, Figure 4).
task.duration: 20 minutes for each selected research topic (p. 18, Appendix I.2).

contrasts.reported: Overall: w. Reference 39.1%; Tie 28.3%; w/o Reference 32.6%. These are expert pairwise preference percentages, not mean quality scores; no test statistic, p-value or interval is reported for this contrast.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Table 6a, Overall row; §6.2, Quality of Ideas; p. 19, Figure 2 (rating criteria).

contrasts.reported: Novelty: w. Reference 43.5%; Tie 23.9%; w/o Reference 32.6%. These are expert pairwise preference percentages, not mean quality scores; no test statistic, p-value or interval is reported for this contrast.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Table 6a, Novelty row; §6.2, Quality of Ideas; p. 19, Figure 2 (rating criteria).

contrasts.reported: Feasibility: w. Reference 50.0%; Tie 17.4%; w/o Reference 32.6%. These are expert pairwise preference percentages, not mean quality scores; no test statistic, p-value or interval is reported for this contrast.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Table 6a, Feasibility row; §6.2, Quality of Ideas; p. 19, Figure 2 (rating criteria).

outcomes.name: Significance of research ideas
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Experts compare the impact of participants’ research ideas on researchers and the broader public (p. 13, Appendix D; p. 19, Figure 2). Ideas are paired within topics across assistance conditions, with additional comparators sampled for surplus ideas; the paper gives no separate count of evaluated units for this outcome (p. 8, §6.2).

contrasts.reported: Significance: w. Reference 39.1%; Tie 21.7%; w/o Reference 39.1%. These are expert pairwise preference percentages, not mean quality scores; no test statistic, p-value or interval is reported for this contrast.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Table 6a, Significance row; §6.2, Quality of Ideas; p. 13, Appendix D; p. 19, Figure 2 (rating criteria).

outcomes.name: Expected effectiveness of research ideas
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Experts compare how likely participants’ ideas are to achieve their intended outcomes, meaning how likely their theories are to be supported by empirical evidence (p. 13, Appendix D; p. 19, Figure 2). Ideas are paired within topics across assistance conditions, with additional comparators sampled for surplus ideas; the paper gives no separate count of evaluated units for this outcome (p. 8, §6.2).

contrasts.reported: Exp. Effectiveness: w. Reference 39.1%; Tie 28.3%; w/o Reference 32.6%. These are expert pairwise preference percentages, not mean quality scores; no test statistic, p-value or interval is reported for this contrast.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Table 6a, Exp. Effectiveness row; §6.2, Quality of Ideas; p. 13, Appendix D; p. 19, Figure 2 (rating criteria).

studies.label: Metadata augmentation of model-generated research ideas (§4)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Model-generation prompts differ in whether CLIMATEDATABANK metadata is supplied. AI-Researcher, GPT-Researcher and Chain-of-Ideas generate the ideas; no people are assigned ideation assistance.
assignment.quote: We preserve each method’s original design while adding metadata to the idea generation prompt.

arms.name: Model generation with metadata
arms.description: AI-Researcher, GPT-Researcher and Chain-of-Ideas each generate research ideas with CLIMATEDATABANK descriptions added to their prompts (p. 4, §4.3). Counts of human ideators do not apply.

arms.name: Model generation without metadata
arms.description: The same model-generation methods operate without the metadata addition (p. 5, Tables 2–3). Counts of human ideators do not apply.

participants.who: The study evaluates model-generated ideas. The 18 recruited human annotators have graduate-level or higher social-science backgrounds; they judge outputs and are not participants producing ideas with or without AI assistance.
participants.quote: We recruit 18 human annotators at the graduate level or above, with academic backgrounds in social science.

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-4o via AI-Researcher, GPT-Researcher and Chain-of-Ideas; Gemini-1.5-Pro and Claude-3.5-Sonnet as judges.
ai_tool.how_used: The generation methods retrieve literature and generate ideas with or without metadata; models rank outputs and experts compare GPT-Researcher outputs (pp. 4–6, §§4.3–4.4).

task.description: Generate 50 ideas per method for each of 10 climate-negotiation topics, then select the top 5 per topic for evaluation (p. 4, §4.3).

studies.label: Reference-based evaluation of model idea selection (§5.2)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Judge models compare published-paper ideas with generated ideas, with and without access to validation processes. The intervention changes model evaluation inputs, not assistance assigned to human participants.
assignment.quote: We prompt LLMs to perform pairwise ranking between ground-truth ideas (extracted from academic papers) and LLM-generated ideas, and compare ranking accuracy with and without access to validation processes.

arms.name: Model ranking with validation
arms.description: Gemini-1.5-Pro and Claude-3.5-Sonnet rank idea pairs with access to validation processes (pp. 6–7, §5.2 and Table 4). Counts of human ideators do not apply.

arms.name: Model ranking without validation
arms.description: The same judge models rank idea pairs without access to validation processes (pp. 6–7, §5.2 and Table 4). Counts of human ideators do not apply.

participants.who: Ideas extracted from 8 published climate-negotiation papers are compared with model-generated ideas. This is a model ranking-accuracy benchmark, not a recruited sample of human ideators.
participants.quote: For each of the 8 climate negotiation papers we collected, we manually extract the research topic and use GPT-Researcher to generate 10 ideas on the same topic, provided with the corresponding dataset description.

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-Researcher using GPT-4o; Gemini-1.5-Pro and Claude-3.5-Sonnet as judges.
ai_tool.how_used: Models judge whether a published-paper idea ranks above an LLM-generated idea; validation access is varied and ranking accuracy is evaluated (pp. 6–7, §5.2).

task.description: Pairwise ranking of published-paper and generated research ideas, with ranking accuracy defined by whether the published-paper idea is ranked higher (p. 7, §5.2).

studies.label: Expert evaluation of model ideas selected with validation (§5.3)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Claude-3.5-Sonnet selects ideas from the same generated candidate pools with and without validation information; humans evaluate the selected ideas rather than receive ideation assistance.
assignment.quote: We then conduct a human evaluation comparing LLM-generated ideas selected with and without validation processes.

arms.name: Model selection with validation
arms.description: Claude-3.5-Sonnet selects ideas using their content and validation processes (p. 7, §5.3). Counts of human ideators do not apply.

arms.name: Model selection without validation
arms.description: Claude-3.5-Sonnet selects ideas using their content alone (p. 7, §5.3). Counts of human ideators do not apply.

participants.who: Human annotators compare model-selected ideas using the setup from §4.4; §5.3 does not give a separate evaluator headcount. There are no human participants producing the research ideas in this experiment.
participants.quote: Human annotators then perform pairwise evaluations of the two sets, using the same evaluation setup as described in §4.4.

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-Researcher using GPT-4o for generation; Claude-3.5-Sonnet for selection.
ai_tool.how_used: Claude-3.5-Sonnet selects research ideas with or without automatic validation; experts then evaluate the resulting selections (p. 7, §5.3).

task.description: Select the top 5 ideas from the 50 GPT-Researcher candidates for each research topic, using idea content alone or content plus validation; experts compare the selected sets (p. 7, §5.3).

studies.label: Pilot benchmark of automatic hypothesis validation (Appendix F)

assignment.what_was_assigned: The model validates hypotheses with corresponding data; a memorization baseline predicts support without access to the data. No human participants are assigned AI assistance.
assignment.quote: To assess whether this performance stems from memorization, we compare it to a memorization baseline, where the LLM is asked to predict whether the hypotheses are supported without access to the data.
assignment.locator: pp. 14–15, Appendix F, Experimental Setup and Results.

arms.name: Model hypothesis validation with data
arms.description: GPT-4o uses a code interpreter and supplied data to validate published hypotheses (p. 15, Appendix F). Counts of human ideators do not apply.

arms.name: Model memorization baseline without data
arms.description: GPT-4o predicts whether hypotheses are supported without access to the data (p. 15, Appendix F, Results). Counts of human ideators do not apply.

participants.who: Benchmark hypotheses are drawn from climate-negotiation papers and DiscoveryBench; domain experts review validation processes. These are not participants producing creative outputs under AI-assistance conditions.
participants.quote: We assess LLMs’ ability to validate hypotheses from published papers.
participants.locator: pp. 14–15, Appendix F, Table 11, Experimental Setup and Results.

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-4o with the code interpreter assistant.
ai_tool.how_used: The model writes and runs Python code over supplied datasets to test hypotheses; a no-data memorization baseline is also evaluated (p. 15, Appendix F).

task.description: Validate hypotheses against published conclusions and evaluate the reasoning processes; this is a model-validation benchmark, not human creative ideation (pp. 14–15, Appendix F).

eligibility.reason: The human ideation study reports 23 recruited people (p. 7, §6.1), below the 50-person threshold; its separately analyzed headcount is not stated and remains null. It describes a within-person comparison but does not state random assignment of topics to references or random condition order (pp. 7–8, §6.1; p. 18, Appendix I.2; p. 25, Figure 4), so criterion 1 is unclear and design_class is other. Random sampling on p. 8, §6.2 is used only to pair surplus ideas for evaluation. Experts score the participants’ actual ideas on overall quality, novelty, feasibility, significance and expected effectiveness (p. 8, §6.2 and Table 6a), meeting criterion 3. S3 compares ideas extracted from published human research with LLM-generated ideas and therefore qualifies as ai_vs_human context under codebook §§3–4 (pp. 6–7, §5.2 and Table 4). Its outcome is judge ranking accuracy, defined as the proportion of comparisons favoring the published idea, with and without access to validation; it supplies no randomized human-assistance evidence. S2, S4 and S5 are model-only benchmarks; evaluator and published-paper counts do not establish a human ideation sample (pp. 4–7, §§4–5; pp. 14–15, Appendix F). No confirmed non-random human allocation is established, so observational context is not assigned. Core eligibility remains no.

one_line_finding: In a study recruiting 23 researchers, expert comparisons favored ideas with AI-generated references on overall quality in 39.1% of comparisons, versus 32.6% favoring ideas without references and 28.3% ties; random assignment and a separate analyzed headcount are not stated (pp. 7–8, §6.1 and Table 6a).
